approved: Moved the Appropriation Bill (No. 4) 2014-2015 seeking just under $241 million, including $90 million for drought recovery concessional loans in Queensland and New South Wales, just over $40 million for a temporary embassy in Ukraine, and just under $35 million for additional counter-terrorism activities.

Moved the Appropriation (Parliamentary Departments) Bill (No. 2) 2014-2015 seeking just under $114 million, primarily to fund upgrades to Parliament House's closed circuit television and access systems and additional parliamentary protective service staff.

Reported that additional appropriation bills worth $1.7 billion reflect a mid-year budget update showing a $44 billion blow-out in the deficit, equivalent to $202 million a day, noted unemployment had risen to 6.4 per cent from 5.7 per cent at the last election, and said the bills incorporate a total $11.3 billion cut to foreign aid.

Defended the government's economic record, citing 213,900 new jobs created last year, equivalent to 585 a day, and a Dun and Bradstreet survey finding the employment outlook the most positive in 10 years, and announced $90 million in additional drought concessional loans on top of the $280 million already committed under the 2014-15 drought package.

Argued a return to a Labor government would restore fairness, describing the debate on the appropriation bills as ultimately a debate on a budget of broken promises, and pointed to the Liberal Party's election manifesto full of commitments it broke.

Criticised the government's $30 billion cut to school education funding and its plan to deregulate university fees, warning the University of Newcastle could lose almost $160 million over four years, and said youth unemployment in the Hunter region stands at 18 per cent, more than double the eight per cent regional rate.

The speaker opposed the government's budget measures, including the GP tax, higher education deregulation, six-month Newstart waiting periods for young job seekers, $5.5 billion in family payment cuts, $270 million in community grants cuts, and pension indexation changes that would cut pensions by $80 a week by 2023-24, citing broken promises by the Prime Minister.
